doc_description: This document presents a rare case study of a 57-year-old woman with acute confusion due to a left-sided hemorrhage, revealing the concurrence of a cavernous malformation, a developmental venous anomaly, and an arteriovenous malformation, while emphasizing the significance of preserving venous outflow during surgical intervention and the evolving understanding of vascular malformations.

structure.title: RESIDENT & FELLOW SECTION
structure.summary: The partial document discusses a case involving a 57-year-old woman who experienced acute confusion due to a left-sided hemorrhage. Imaging studies, including CT and MRI, revealed a cavernous malformation (CM) associated with a complex developmental venous anomaly (DVA) and an arteriovenous malformation (AVM) draining into the DVA. The concurrence of these three vascular malformations is noted to be exceptionally rare. The document emphasizes the importance of preserving DVA outflow during AVM removal and highlights the evolving understanding of the venous system's role in the development of vascular malformations. Additionally, it includes imaging features of the identified malformations and provides information about the authors' affiliations and the publication details.

RESIDENT & FELLOW SECTION
Teaching NeuroImages: The Venous System and
Developmental Venous Anomalies
Drivers of Vascular Malformations?
Anthony S. Larson, BS, Harry Cloft, MD, PhD, Ivan D. Carabenciov, MD, and Giuseppe Lanzino, MD
Neurology ®2021;96:e960-e961. doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000010815Correspondence
Anthony S. Larson
lars4689@umn.edu
A 57-year-old woman presented with acute con fusion. CT-scan showed a left-sided hem-
orrhage, and MR-imaging demonstrated an adjacent cavernous malformation (CM) associ-ated with a complex developmental venous anomaly (DVA) continuous with the hemorrhage
(ﬁgure, A –C). Digital subtraction angiography demo nstrated an arteriovenous malformation
(AVM) draining into the DVA ( ﬁgure, D –F). DVAs are typically-benign lesions commonly
associated with CMs and rarely, AVMs.
1Concurrence of these 3 malformations is excep-
tionally rare. Preserving DVA out ﬂow is crucial when AVM extirpation is indicated.1Our
understanding of the role of the venous system and DVAs in the genesis of vascular mal-
formations continues to evolve.2Figure Imaging Features of a CM Concurrent with DVA and AVM
(A)) Left-hemispheric hemorrhage. MRI/MRA suggestive of a (B) CM (arrow) and (C) DVA (arrow). (D)) A basal ganglia
AVM (arrows) with (E) an intranidal aneurysm (arrow), the likely source of hemorrhage. (F) )3-D angiography showing
the DVA with smaller veins (solid arrows) and a larger collecting vein (dashed arrow). AVM = arteriovenous malfor-
mation; CM = cavernous malformation; DVA = developmental venous anomaly.
From the Department of Radiology (A.S.L., H.C., G.L.); Department of Neurosurgery (G.L.); and Department of Neurology (I.D.C.), Mayo Clinic, Roche ster, MN.

nodes.title: Drivers of Vascular Malformations?
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses a case study involving a 57-year-old woman who experienced acute confusion due to a left-sided hemorrhage. Imaging techniques, including CT and MRI, revealed a cavernous malformation (CM) associated with a complex developmental venous anomaly (DVA) and an arteriovenous malformation (AVM). The document highlights the rarity of the concurrence of these three vascular malformations and emphasizes the importance of preserving DVA outflow during AVM removal. It also notes the evolving understanding of the venous system's role in the development of vascular malformations. The authors, affiliated with the Mayo Clinic, contributed to the study's design, data analysis, and manuscript preparation. The document includes references to relevant literature and acknowledges the absence of targeted funding or disclosures.
